newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon says Netanyahu has not shown he wants peace.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon says Netanyahu has not shown he wants peace.

text.p: Lebanon's Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri said on Wednesday Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had not yet shown that he was a man in search of peace or a man to be trusted.
In an interview with Reuters, Hariri said Israel must resume peace talks where they left off last year and return all occupied Syrian and Lebanese land if it wanted peace.
"The way Mr Netanyahu is acting, I am telling you he is not building real confidence. (He is) looking at small details, saying one thing today and something else tomorrow.
"He doesn't give a constant idea, a real clear idea of a man who is looking for peace," Hariri said.
He said Netanyahu's behaviour over the West Bank town of Hebron, insisting on re-negotiating the agreement and delaying its handover to the Palestinians, had given the Arabs a bad impression.
"It gave a bad idea about the behaviour, the thinking of Prime Minister Netanyahu," Hariri said.

"So far Mr Netanyahu did not show that he is a real believer in peace. I hope he will change. I hope he will go for peace because it is good for everybody...for the Jews as well as the Arabs," he added.
Israel handed over control of 80 percent of Hebron to Palestinian self-rule Authority last week after months of difficult negotiations.
Hariri, a 52-year-old billionaire construction tycoon, said that if Netanyahu really wanted peace "he has to withdraw from Lebanon and from the (Syrian) Golan Heights, totally and completely".
"(But) if he wants to dominate the region, as he has shown that he wants to dominate the Palestinians so far, I think peace will be very far off," Hariri said.
"If he really believes in peace he has to start the negotiations from the point at which they stopped."
Israel broke off talks last year after a series of bombings by Moslem militants killed 59 people in Israel and Netanyahu has since rejected the land-for-peace formula on which they were based.
Hariri, who has held office for more than four years, has made several strides towards rebuilding Lebanon after its devastating 1975-90 civil war.

He has restored government control in most of Lebanon with the help of 35,000 Syrian troops, but war still rages in the south between Moslem guerrillas and Israeli troops occupying a border strip comprising about 10 percent of Lebanon's territory.

Hariri's government has repeatedly said the 63,000-strong Lebanese army could take control of the south whenever the Israelis withdraw and prevent cross-border attacks against Israel, but negotiations on a pullout have been stalled for years.

Although Lebanon is Syria's closest ally, Hariri has struck a moderate posture on international issues and has moved steadily closer to Washington in the past four years. He said relations with the United States, which last month hosted a donors' conference for Lebanon, were now "more than good".
However, Hariri complained that Netanyahu had been giving conflicting signals about his intentions on the key issue of an Israeli withdrawal from the Golan Heights.
"He said a few days ago he doesn't want to withdraw from the Golan Heights. And then yesterday he said 'No, I don't mean that'. We don't know what he will say today.

"What I am saying is that a deal needs confidence. To build confidence you have to be constant and you have to show interest in peace....We have to behave as people who believe deeply in peace," Hariri said.
